narrative:
**HEADLINE**
Macro risk closes at High, driven by structural leverage and geopolitical supply-chain vulnerabilities with no intraday shifts.

**KEY STORIES**
No stories moved today. Fourteen risks remain elevated or higher:

• **High-band risks:** Private credit's opaque expansion (8), Sea lanes & undersea cables (8), Japan fiscal/JGB/carry trade (7), and Critical minerals as a weapon (7) persist as the sharpest pressure points.

• **Elevated risks:** Treasury basis trade hidden leverage, Developing-world debt crisis, China's price spillover, AI build-out circular financing, AI power & grid bottleneck, Food & fertilizer fragility, and The lithography chokepoint all remain stable at level 6. France/eurozone fragility, Hidden consumer debt, and Water underpricing hold at level 5.

**WATCH**
Private credit's opaque expansion at High (8) and Sea lanes & undersea cables at High (8) demand closest monitoring for sudden repricing or disruption events.

stories.name: Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)

indicators.label: SOFR minus EFFR (%)
MOVE index (Treasury volatility)
SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)

stories.summary: Hedge funds run a highly leveraged arbitrage between Treasury cash bonds and futures. It is a major source of liquidity, but a spike in funding costs or Treasury volatility can force rapid unwinds, as briefly happened in March 2020 and again in 2025.

stories.name: Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade

indicators.label: USD/JPY (yen strengthening = lower = risk)
30-year JGB yield (%)
Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)

stories.summary: Decades of near-zero rates made Japan the funding leg of a vast global carry trade. As the BoJ normalizes and JGB yields rise, fiscal financing gets harder and carry unwinds can transmit stress worldwide - the August 2024 mini-crash was a preview.

stories.name: Private credit's opaque expansion

indicators.label: US high-yield OAS (%, ≈310bps)
Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

stories.summary: Lending has migrated from banks to lightly regulated private-credit funds, where assets are marked infrequently and leverage is opaque. Defaults are rising from a low base; the risk is that losses surface suddenly rather than being visible in real time.

stories.name: Developing-world debt crisis

indicators.label: Broad US dollar index (FRED DTWEXBGS)
US 10y real yield (TIPS, %)
New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A strong dollar, high real rates, and heavy foreign-currency debt loads leave many developing economies vulnerable to a sudden stop. A cluster of sovereign defaults or new IMF programs would signal the slow-burn crisis turning acute.

stories.name: China's price spillover (deflation or cost-push)

indicators.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
USD/CNY (yuan depreciation = higher = risk)
New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

stories.summary: China's factory-gate prices spill into global goods markets in BOTH directions: years of PPI deflation exported disinflation and squeezed competitors, while a sharp 2026 reversal to positive PPI (energy/commodity cost-push) now exports input-cost pressure. Either large swing is destabilising; the indicator is scored on the size of the move, not its sign.

stories.name: Critical minerals as a weapon

indicators.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

stories.summary: China dominates the mining and especially the processing of rare earths and critical minerals, and has shown willingness to use export licensing as leverage. Supply chains for magnets and defense inputs have little near-term substitute.

stories.name: Stablecoins & Treasury demand

indicators.label: Largest stablecoin max peg deviation (%)
Total USD stablecoin supply ($bn)
GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Dollar stablecoins have become sizeable holders of short-term Treasuries, linking crypto plumbing to the funding market. A large redemption wave could force rapid T-bill selling; the GENIUS Act's implementation is the key regulatory variable.

stories.name: AI build-out circular financing

indicators.label: US investment-grade OAS (%) - big-issuer proxy
AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)

stories.summary: AI infrastructure spending vastly exceeds current AI revenue, increasingly financed with debt and circular vendor arrangements. If monetization disappoints or GPU-backed financing strains, the capex cycle could reverse sharply.

stories.name: CRE maturity wall / regional banks

indicators.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A wall of commercial real-estate loans - especially office - matures into higher rates and lower valuations, concentrated at regional banks. Rising delinquencies and 'extend and pretend' practices defer, rather than resolve, the losses.

stories.name: France / eurozone fragility

indicators.label: OAT-Bund 10y spread (%)
Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

stories.summary: France combines a wide deficit, a fragmented parliament, and recurring budget standoffs, widening its spread over Germany. Political instability or a rating downgrade would test eurozone cohesion at its second-largest economy.

stories.name: Hidden consumer debt

indicators.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
US unemployment rate (%)
BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)

stories.summary: Beneath headline figures, subprime auto and buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are climbing, and the labor market is the swing factor. A rise in unemployment would convert stretched-but-current borrowers into defaults quickly.

stories.name: Gold / de-dollarization

indicators.label: Gold price (USD/oz)
USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

stories.summary: Central banks are accumulating gold and building non-dollar settlement arrangements at the margin. It is a slow erosion rather than a sudden shift, but reserve 'weaponization' events can accelerate diversification away from the dollar.

stories.name: Insurance retreat

indicators.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
US single-family mortgage delinquency (%, FRED DRSFRMACBS)
Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)

stories.summary: Insurers are retreating from climate-exposed markets through non-renewals and exits, shifting risk onto homeowners and state backstops. Severe catastrophe seasons strain the system and feed into housing and mortgage stress.

stories.name: Pensions / demographics

indicators.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
Large public-pension funded ratio (%)

stories.summary: Aging demographics and underfunded public pensions create slow fiscal pressure, while leveraged liability-driven strategies can blow up fast - as the UK gilt/LDI crisis showed in 2022. Benefit-reform fights are the political pressure valve.

stories.name: AI power & the grid bottleneck

indicators.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)

stories.summary: Data-center electricity demand is colliding with multi-year grid interconnection queues and slow capacity additions. Whether this is an acute shortfall or eases depends on the pace of AI build-out versus new supply - forecasts diverge widely.

stories.name: Copper & the electrification deficit

indicators.label: Copper price (USD/lb, COMEX HG=F)
Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)

stories.summary: Electrification and AI infrastructure point to structural copper deficits as demand outruns new mine supply, which takes a decade to build. Price is the live signal; mine disruptions and inventory draws would confirm tightening.

stories.name: Water - the underpriced input

indicators.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

stories.summary: Water is systematically underpriced yet essential to chip fabrication, agriculture, and power. Droughts in key hubs (Taiwan's fabs, major farming regions) and transboundary disputes can disrupt supply chains in ways markets rarely price in advance.

stories.name: Food & fertilizer fragility

indicators.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)

stories.summary: Food security depends on concentrated fertilizer supply chains - potash, phosphate, and gas-derived nitrogen - exposed to export curbs and shipping chokepoints. Curbs or input shocks feed through to prices with a lag.

stories.name: The lithography (ASML) chokepoint

indicators.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

stories.summary: ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography machines, with Zeiss the sole optics supplier - a single point of failure for advanced chips. Export controls, retaliation, or any disruption to this chain would ripple across the entire tech economy.

stories.name: Sea lanes & undersea cables

indicators.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
WTI crude oil (USD/bbl, CL=F)
Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

stories.summary: A few maritime chokepoints and undersea cables carry most global trade and data. The 2026 Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions showed how quickly closures spike energy and shipping costs; cable cuts are a parallel, under-watched vulnerability.

stories.name: Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)

indicators.label: Equity volatility (VIX)
Treasury volatility (MOVE)
Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Central counterparties now concentrate the system's risk by design, and Treasury central-clearing mandates will route more activity through them. In a volatility spike, procyclical margin calls can amplify stress - they are a systemic single point of failure.

items.label: Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
items.rationale: Fitch's inclusive TTM measure (counting distressed exchanges and maturity extensions) printed 6.3% for August 2026, eclipsing the prior record of 6.1% in July and the April 2026 record of 6.0%; this is the mandated anchor per the rubric and no anchor switch is required as a fresh Fitch print is available. The rate trajectory (5.6% Dec-2025 → 5.8% Jan → 6.0% Apr → 6.1% Jul → 6.3% Aug) signals sustained and accelerating credit deterioration in private direct lending, consistent with elevated PIK income at BDCs and maturity-extension-dominated default events.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings reported today (September 14, 2026) that the trailing 12-month US private credit default rate rose to 6.3% at end of August 2026, a new record surpassing the prior month's 6.1%, per Bloomberg citing Fitch's report released Monday. Source: https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-14/us-private-credit-default-rate-hits-a-record-of-6-3-fitch-says

dissent.view: Proskauer Private Credit Default Index (count-based, senior secured/unitranche only) reported 2.51% for Q2 2026 across 716 loans representing $195.6B — roughly 3.8 points below Fitch's inclusive rate
Moody's estimated 2025 private credit headline default rates of 1.6%–4.7% excluding distressed exchanges, with distressed restructurings accounting for ~65% of all 2025 private credit defaults
IMF April 2026 Global Financial Stability Report described private credit default rates in the 2–3% range as 'manageable in magnitude'

items.label: GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The July 18, 2026 statutory deadline was missed with zero final rules published by any primary regulator — this maps squarely to rubric level 2 ('deadline missed without final rules'). The Act's effective date now defaults to the January 18, 2027 backstop, and Treasury continued issuing new NPRMs in August 2026 with comment periods running to October 2026, confirming no imminent finalization.
items.fact: The GENIUS Act Section 13 statutory rulemaking deadline was July 18, 2026. As of that date and through at least mid-August 2026, zero agencies (OCC, FDIC, Federal Reserve, NCUA, Treasury, FinCEN, OFAC) had issued final implementing rules — every workstream remained at the NPRM/proposed stage. Treasury published a further NPRM on stablecoin issuance in August 2026 with comments due October 19, 2026 (Federal Register, 2026-08-18). Sources: coinpaprika.com (July 19-20 2026), astraea.law (July 18 2026), federalregister.gov (August 18 2026), fdic.gov (April 2026 NPRM), occ.gov (NPRM bulletin 2026-3), home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0605.

dissent.view: Paradigm and Chapman & Cutler note agencies face 'no formal penalties' for missing the rulemaking deadline and the GENIUS Act still takes effect January 18, 2027 via the 18-month backstop, suggesting operational continuity rather than a crisis scenario.
Astraea Counsel characterizes the missed deadline as a rulemaking slip, not an Act-effectiveness failure, since the January 18, 2027 statutory backstop remains intact.

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: The rubric threshold for level 2 is >=3 of the largest funds gating, or combined AUM >$100B; at least 5 named large funds—including BCRED ($79B) and Cliffwater CCLFX ($31B) alone exceeding $100B combined—hit their quarterly repurchase caps in Q2 2026, with 10/16 Fitch-tracked BDCs breaching caps in the same quarter, far exceeding the widespread threshold.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings data (cited by multiple trade sources as of Aug 17 2026) shows 10 of 16 tracked BDCs breached their 5% quarterly repurchase caps in Q2 2026; named funds with active gates include Blackstone BCRED (~$79B AUM, gated Jun 4 2026), Blue Owl OTIC (38.1% request rate, paid ~12 cents on dollar), Cliffwater CCLFX (~$31B, 17% requests vs 5% honored), Apollo Debt Solutions BDC (~$26B, 11%+ requests), and Morgan Stanley North Haven Private Income Fund (~$7B, 11.6% requests). R.A. Stanger pegs Q2 requests at 12.4% of NAV industry-wide, with only 38% fulfilled and ~$9.6B left unmet.

dissent.view: iCapital (Mar 2026) argued funds were honoring 100% of tenders even when requests exceeded 5%, characterising the episode as sentiment-driven rather than structural; early Q3 data (Golub GCRED cleared July tender in full at 4.8%) suggest some easing in Q3 2026

items.label: Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)
items.rationale: The 10-year yield is materially elevated on fiscal concern (cumulative rise well above 25bps) and the financing path for the consumption-tax cut is unspecified, satisfying the UNCLEAR criteria; however, no auction has failed (bid-to-cover <2) and no emergency BOJ operation has been documented, so the DISORDERLY threshold is not met.
items.fact: Japan 10-year JGB yield reached 2.99% on Sep 11, 2026 (Trading Economics / MoF), up ~15bps from the Sep 1 auction stop of 2.840% and cumulatively >50bps above mid-2026 levels, driven by Takaichi fiscal-stimulus concerns and BOJ rate-hike expectations; the Sep 1 10-year auction cleared at a yield of 2.995% with no reported failed bid-to-cover or emergency BOJ operation; Takaichi's May supplementary budget promised no new net bond issuance but her food-tax-cut financing path remains unspecified (CNBC, Aug 4 2026).

dissent.view: Lazard (Jun 2026) notes Takaichi has actively tempered fiscal stimulus expectations to reassure bond markets, implying the yield rise is as much BOJ normalisation-driven as fiscal-shock-driven, which would soften the fiscal-stress reading toward 0.

items.label: Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)
items.rationale: No deadline extension has been granted (ruling out score 2), but a documented legal/documentation backlog for bilateral repo agreements plus multiple pending exemptive relief requests (SIFMA inter-affiliate, IIB cross-border, 15c3-3 net omnibus margin) squarely satisfy the rubric definition of FRICTION: documentation backlog and pending exemptive relief. Cash side is better positioned but repo readiness remains materially incomplete with $300-400B still to migrate on cash alone. [vintage guard: new read is 2026-08-07 data but the prior applied value was 2026-08 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: DTCC/FICC July 2026 readiness survey (sent to all GSD Netting Members) found most respondents 'already prepared or actively completing final readiness activities,' with 79% having required FICC account structures in place and ~$1.2T/day already clearing, but ~$300-400B/day cash still to be onboarded; TBAC May 2026 charge identified 'the largest challenge from an implementation standpoint continues to be the amount of legal work and documentation associated with the bilateral agreements'; SEC August 7 2026 statement (sec.gov) confirmed a 15c3-3 net-omnibus-margin exemptive relief request still open for comment (due Aug 31 2026) and SIFMA/IIB inter-affiliate exemptive relief requests still pending. No further deadline extension has been announced. Primary sources: DTCC/Finadium July 27 2026 (finadium.com/ficc-survey-shows-ust-clearing-at-scale-ahead-of-sec-deadline/); TBAC Charge Q2 2026 (home.treasury.gov/system/files/221/TBACCharge1Q22026.pdf); SEC Uyeda statement Aug 7 2026 (sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/uyeda-statement-update-secs-work-toward-treasury-clearing-implementation-080726).

dissent.view: DTCC/FICC and SEC chair Atkins (March 2026) characterize the industry as 'well positioned' for the Dec 31 2026 cash deadline, suggesting a possible score of 0 for cash-specific readiness; however repo documentation backlog and open regulatory relief requests prevent a clean 'smooth' reading.

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth (~77% YoY aggregate) exceeds AI-cloud revenue growth for AWS (+37%) and Azure (+43%), keeping the monetization gap WIDE. However, all three hyperscalers show QoQ acceleration in AI-revenue (Google Cloud 63%->82%, AWS 28%->37%), ruling out level 2 (WIDENING FAST), which requires deceleration or an outlook cut.
items.fact: Q2 2026 actuals: Google Cloud +82% YoY to $24.8B (accelerating from +63% in Q1), AWS +37% YoY to $42.2B (accelerating from +28% in Q1), Azure +43% YoY. Combined 2026 hyperscaler capex raised to ~$725-740B (+77% YoY from ~$410B in 2025), with Amazon raising to ~$220B, Alphabet to $195-205B, Meta to $130-145B. Sources: company Q2 2026 earnings releases; Synergy Research Q2 2026; uncoveralpha.com (Aug 3 2026); fourweekmba.com (Jul 31 2026).

dissent.view: Google Cloud alone grew 82% YoY in Q2 2026, which exceeds the ~77% aggregate capex growth rate, suggesting the gap may be CLOSING for Alphabet specifically; Alphabet also raised capex ceiling to $205B at Q2 earnings, partially offsetting this.

Pre-Q2 analysis (July 20 2026) flagged that 'the buildout is accelerating faster than the monetisation curve' and cited Moody's May 2026 credit-risk warning if AI profit growth fails to materialise, a more bearish framing closer to level 2.

items.label: BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: Affirm 30+ DPD rose 29 bps YoY to 2.8% — above flat but well below the 100 bps spike threshold; projected charge-offs ~3.5% are below the 5% spiking threshold, fitting rubric level 1 (RISING, charge-offs contained). Klarna provisions are essentially flat YoY, providing no systemic escalation signal.
items.fact: Affirm FQ3'26 Shareholder Letter (SEC 8-K, May 7 2026, period ending March 31 2026): '30+ day delinquencies excluding Peloton and Pay in X loans increased 29 basis points year over year ... to 2.8%'; allowance for credit losses 6.0% of loans held for investment; projected ultimate net charge-offs ~3.5% of cohort GMV, in-line with expectations. Klarna Q1 2026 credit-loss provisions 0.55% of GMV vs 0.54% YoY. Source: https://investors.affirm.com/static-files/5a0ae9e1-e495-4030-b115-b7d5a502e5e6

dissent.view: Benzinga/SahmCapital (June 2 2026) characterises Affirm 30+ DPD as 'flat against a year earlier at 2.8%', understating the +29 bps YoY move documented in the primary SEC filing

LendingTree survey (March 2026) puts 47% of BNPL users as having paid late in the past year (up from 41% in 2025 and 34% in 2024), a far harsher characterisation than lender balance-sheet data, but is a self-reported survey not a hard delinquency rate

items.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
items.rationale: The rubric requires the latest published Trepp CMBS office delinquency percent; the hardest confirmed Trepp office figure is 11.76% (Oct 2025 all-time high), with July 2026 Trepp data showing continued office stress but no office sub-rate extractable from available sources, yielding medium confidence. KBRA data for early 2026 (12.8%–13.9%) and S&P paywalled headline (>10.5% in Jan 2026) are consistent with an elevated but uncertain 2026 Trepp office rate. [vintage guard: new read is 2025-10 data but the prior applied value was 2026-03 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: Trepp CMBS office delinquency rate jumped 63 bps in October 2025 to set a new all-time high of 11.76% (source: commercialsearch.com/news/cmbs-delinquency-rates/, reporting Trepp data, published ~Nov 2025). The July 2026 overall Trepp CMBS rate surged to 7.86% (+51 bps) driven in part by a Chicago office tower and a Seattle office portfolio going delinquent, but a Trepp office-specific sub-rate for 2026 was not available in retrievable excerpts.

dissent.view: KBRA office CMBS delinquency rate was 13.9% in January 2026, falling to 12.8% in February 2026 — materially higher than the Trepp figure, reflecting KBRA-rated universe differences and the One New York Plaza ($835M) maturity default event
S&P Global Ratings headline states the office CMBS rate 'surpasses 10.5%' in January 2026 (paywalled), implying a lower reading than KBRA under S&P's universe definition

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: CoreWeave is a named borrower facing a documented 2026 refinancing wall on GPU-backed debt with sharply widening CDS spreads (855 bps, distressed-tier), satisfying Rubric 1 ('a named borrower facing a refinancing wall'). No confirmed default, failed refinancing, or distressed exchange has been reported — the $2.6B loan cleared after sweetened terms — so Rubric 2 is not triggered.
items.fact: On July 29, 2026, CoreWeave's 5-year CDS spread hit ~855 bps (implying ~50% default probability), a level associated with distressed borrowers; the company then had to sweeten terms to place a $2.6 billion leveraged loan tied to Anthropic. CoreWeave also carries a $4.2 billion pre-Meta refinancing wall due in 2026 on GPU-backed debt where collateral values have declined. No confirmed default or distressed exchange has occurred; Q2 2026 revenue beat at $2.1B+ and the $2.6B loan ultimately cleared. Sources: Bloomberg (2026-03-31, 2026-07-29), metirai.com/CDS analysis (2026-08-02), capacityglobal.com (2026-08-12), davefriedman.substack.com (2026-04-19).

dissent.view: CoreWeave's Q2 2026 revenue beat (+200% YoY, $104B backlog) and successful loan placement suggest refinancing stress is manageable and not acute; equity analysts maintain Buy ratings with ~$145 avg target.

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
items.rationale: 13 confirmed states with active non-renewal waves places the indicator squarely in the 5-15 state 'RISING' band (rubric score 1); no evidence of a confirmed full top-10 insurer exit from a major state market in 2026 itself, and AM Best's stable outlook plus FL Citizens contraction signals some markets are stabilizing rather than accelerating.
items.fact: ClimateCosmos (June 2026) identifies 13 US states with active home-insurer non-renewal waves in 2026, including CA, FL, LA, TX, CO, GA, OK, and NE; corroborated by RollingOut (Sep 5 2026) and NAIC-sourced data showing FL non-renewal rate of 3.35% and CA at 3.18% (2024, per leadgen-economy.com June 2026). State Farm not writing new policies in CA, MA, RI (US News Sep 2026); Farmers absent from FL, HI, and 8 other states. AM Best upgraded homeowners segment outlook from negative to stable Dec 2025, and FL Citizens fell from 1.42M to ~390K policies by Jan 2026, indicating partial stabilization in some markets.

dissent.view: ClimateCosmos (non-authoritative, AI-adjacent content site) lists 13 states but without DOI or AM Best citation; the DOI/AM Best primary anchor is indirect via NAIC 2024 data with a 12-month lag, so the true 2026 count could differ.
AM Best upgraded homeowners P&C market outlook to stable in Dec 2025, suggesting the withdrawal wave may be past its peak rather than still 'rising'.

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Zero FDIC bank failures in the trailing 6 months (March-September 2026) and no formal supervisory statement or enforcement action officially citing regional-bank CRE concentration satisfies the CALM rubric (score=0). The sole 2026 failure pre-dates the window and lacks an official CRE-cause determination, preventing elevation to ISOLATED.
items.fact: FDIC failed-bank list (last updated 2026-08-21) shows exactly ONE bank failure in all of 2026: Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust, Chicago, closed 2026-01-30, $261.1M assets. That failure falls outside the trailing-6-month window (2026-03-14 to 2026-09-14). Regulators cited 'unsafe and unsound conditions and an impaired capital position'; no official FDIC/OCC/Fed post-seizure analysis has named CRE concentration as the cause. Bisnow (2026-02-02) reported court records show a troubled real-estate-linked loan as a contributing factor, but this is credible press inference, not a formal supervisory determination. No coordinated interagency CRE enforcement action has been identified. Source: https://www.fdic.gov/bank-failures/failed-bank-list (updated 2026-08-21); https://www.bisnow.com/national/news/capital-markets/cre-tied-to-first-bank-failure-of-2026-133023 (2026-02-02).

dissent.view: Bisnow/The Real Deal (2026-02-02) infer CRE loan exposure as a material contributor to the Metropolitan Capital failure based on court records, which would support an ISOLATED reading if that failure were counted within the rubric window or if the CRE link were officially confirmed.

items.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
items.rationale: The Fitch ABS index is the primary authoritative source for this metric; 5.67% is the latest month (June 2026) with a hard reported figure, mapping directly to the rubric's request for the latest subprime auto 60+ day delinquency rate as a percent.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings subprime auto ABS 60-day-plus delinquency rate in June 2026 was 5.67%, down 64 basis points year-over-year, per Wolf Street citing Fitch (published August 13, 2026).

dissent.view: 5.49% in May 2026 (lowest since May 2024) per ankso.blog citing Fitch — slightly lower than June figure, possibly a May datapoint before seasonal uptick
6.80% in February 2026 per TradingEconomics/Fitch — earlier in the year before seasonal improvement

items.label: Large public-pension funded ratio (%)
items.rationale: The Milliman PPFI is the authoritative monthly mark-to-market index for the 100 largest U.S. public DB plans; 88.2% is the most recent published reading (July 31, 2026) and maps directly to the rubric's request for a representative large-plan funded ratio. Equable's FY2026 actuarial projection of 85.0% and NASRA median of ~73-75% are alternative measures on different methodological bases but are less current.
items.fact: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index (PPFI): the funded ratio of the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans was 88.2% as of July 31, 2026, down from 88.7% as of June 30, 2026. Source: Milliman / BusinessWire, published August 27, 2026. https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260827829119/en/Milliman-analysis-Public-pension-funded-ratio-slips-again-to-88.2-as-of-July-31

dissent.view: Equable Institute 'State of Pensions 2026' projects the national funded ratio at 85.0% for FY2026 (actuarial basis, 253 plans, best level since 2009)
NASRA median funded ratio approximately 73-75% for 2024-2025 (median across all public plans, broader universe, actuarial basis)

items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: One to two sovereigns (Bolivia SLA, Kenya new-program request) entered new-distress-program territory in the window, with no confirmed missed coupons; this is consistent with RISING (1-2 new IMF arrangements) rather than CALM or CLUSTER.
items.fact: In the trailing 6 months (Mar–Sep 2026): Bolivia reached a staff-level agreement for a new EFF on Jul 29 2026 (IMF.org PR, awaiting Board approval); Kenya formally requested a new IMF program after abandoning its 9th review under the existing ECF/EFF (Reuters/Yahoo Finance, 2026); no Board-approved brand-new sovereign programs or confirmed missed coupon/standstill events were found in the window. Existing programs for Argentina (2nd review, May 21 2026) and Ukraine (1st review, Jul 20 2026) are ongoing reviews, not new arrangements.

dissent.view: Bolivia SLA is not yet Board-approved; Kenya has only submitted a request with no approval—stricter reading could argue 0 new formally approved programs, implying CALM (0)

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: Both TPR and ESMA confirm materially improved buffers, lower leverage, and no active margin-stress episode in 2026; the rubric condition for score 0 (LDI buffers adequate, no margin stress, cited by TPR/ESMA) is satisfied. ESMA notes a residual tail risk for a subset of funds under a large shock, but this is a structural caveat in a stress-test paper, not an active regulatory flag of stress, so it does not elevate the score to 1.
items.fact: ESMA June 2026 stress-test paper (esma.europa.eu, pub. June 2026) finds LDI fund liquidity shortfall under stress fell from EUR 9bn to EUR 3bn by end-2024; TPR market-oversight report (thepensionsregulator.gov.uk, data to March 2025) confirms LDI market shrank from ~GBP 1.5tn to ~GBP 0.7tn, rate buffers raised to ~300 bps, and daily volatility in leveraged LDI assets is >50% lower than end-2021. items.label: Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

Moody's negative outlook (Oct-2025) would independently satisfy band 1, but the executed cuts by Fitch and S&P set the highest applicable band.
items.fact: S&P Global Ratings downgraded France from AA- to A+ with a stable outlook on 17 October 2025 (S&P press release; sourceId/101651950); Fitch Ratings separately downgraded France from AA- to A+ in September 2025 (Bloomberg, 2025-09-12); Moody's maintained Aa3 but revised outlook to negative on 24-25 October 2025. As of 28 August 2026, Fitch reaffirmed A+ / stable (Bloomberg, 2026-08-28).

Fitch on 28 Aug 2026 reaffirmed A+ with STABLE outlook, suggesting no further deterioration since the Sep-2025 cut.

items.label: Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)
items.rationale: The BRICS Pay formal summit launch is a new non-dollar settlement agreement/launch — Band 1 by the rubric. The EU indefinite freeze is an escalation of the existing 2022 freeze, not a new completed sovereign seizure (title has not transferred), so it does not meet the Band 2 threshold of a new reserve freeze/seizure or a major economy operationally moving reserve settlement off USD.
items.fact: At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on 12 September 2026, BRICS leaders formally adopted BRICS Pay — a payment-messaging network integrating India's UPI, China's CIPS, Russia's SPFS, and Brazil's Pix — as a new non-dollar cross-border settlement layer (Eastern Herald, 12 Sept 2026). Separately, the EU's Dec 12 2025 vote made the ~€210-230bn Russian central bank asset freeze indefinite, but full confiscation/title transfer has not been executed; Russia filed suit in the EU General Court on 8 Sept 2026 to annul the freeze (kohenavocats.com, 13 Sept 2026).

dissent.view: Some sources (watcher.guru, informedclearly.com) characterise BRICS Pay as already 'operational' with intra-bloc USD usage sharply reduced, which could argue for Band 2 if one reads it as a major economy operationally moving reserve settlement off USD; however these sources are lower-authority aggregators and BIS/official data still show USD on one side of ~89% of FX turnover.

The EU's Dec 12 2025 indefinite-freeze Council decision has been characterised by Fair Observer and Modern Diplomacy as a shift 'from temporary sanctions to potentially permanent seizure,' which some analysts read as meeting a Band 2 threshold; however legal title has not transferred and actual confiscation has not been executed.

items.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
items.rationale: At +3.8% YoY, China PPI is in positive cost-push territory — not deflation, but a moderate positive reading. The rubric scores on SIZE of move; +3.8% is a notable positive print reflecting upstream commodity and energy price pressure with potential to export input-cost inflation to trading partners.
items.fact: China PPI for industrial products rose +3.8% year-on-year in August 2026, per NBS release dated 9 September 2026 (Xinhua: 'China's producer price index (PPI)...went up 3.8 percent year on year in August, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) said Wednesday'). Source: https://english.news.cn/20260909/08bda30608aa431e9c6f830a7deced63/c.html and https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/china-cpi-ppi-august-oil-prices-tech-manufacturing-.html

items.label: Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
items.rationale: Both sides have enacted or sustained formal measures in the trailing window: the US legislative MATCH Act escalation targeting ASML DUV/servicing plus executive-branch pressure on ASML (TIGHTENING), and China's April 2026 supply-chain security regulations plus rare-earth export controls constitute documented formal countermeasures (RETALIATION), satisfying rubric level 2. items.fact: MATCH Act (introduced April 2, 2026) remains in congressional review targeting ASML DUV sales and servicing to China; China enacted 'Regulations on Industrial Chain and Supply Chain Security' in April 2026 (CSIS, April 17, 2026) and maintains rare earth export licensing controls (holmium, thulium, ytterbium) as active countermeasures. US Commerce Secretary Lutnick privately pressed ASML executives from April 2026 onward over alleged EUV diversion (Asia Times, July 11, 2026). Sources: CSIS (csis.org/analysis/new-momentum-old-problems, June 11 2026); Asia Times (July 11, 2026); TechPowerUp (Aug 2026).

dissent.view: MATCH Act is still a bill, not a final BIS rule — no new Federal Register export control measure was issued specifically in June-Sept 2026, which could support rating of 1 (TIGHTENING) rather than 2 if China's April 2026 supply-chain regulations are deemed pre-period or non-semiconductor-specific
ASML CFO downplayed rare-earth control impact and China revenue remained ~20% of 2026 sales, suggesting market signals do not fully corroborate a severe disruption at level 2

items.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
items.rationale: Transit volume at ~7% of baseline (6 vs ~85 ships/day) is well below the rubric's 25% threshold for closure, and Brent at ~$108-110/bbl — up ~60% YoY — provides the required corroborating market signal; no functioning convoy workaround or signed truce is in place (GCC-Iran talks were postponed by Tehran), satisfying all conditions for a score of 2.
items.fact: IMF PortWatch recorded 6 transits on 2026-09-06 vs a pre-crisis baseline of ~85/day (straits.live, 2026-09-14); Brent crude stood at ~$108-110/bbl on 2026-09-14, up ~60-64% year-on-year (TradingEconomics / Fortune, 2026-09-14). The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed to commercial shipping since 28 Feb 2026 following the US-Israel air campaign on Iran; Iran declared it closed to 'unfriendly nations' and laid sea mines (Wikipedia / straits.live). Houthis simultaneously seized Greater and Lesser Hanish islands on 2026-09-14, tightening their grip on Bab el-Mandeb / Red Sea (Washington Times / AP, 2026-09-14).

dissent.view: A brief ceasefire framework in April 2026 and periodic GCC-Iran diplomatic contacts could arguaby cap the rating at 1 (contested), but Iran postponed the Oman talks and the strait remains physically blocked with no operational convoy system running.

items.label: New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

Jul 24 (China Briefing/Congress.gov CRS, Jul 2026); (2) US proposed 7.5% overcapacity tariff on China, Bloomberg Aug 24 2026; (3) China 54.3% provisional anti-dumping on US pecans, MOFCOM Aug 11 2026; (4) China drone export controls + 6 US entity bans, MOFCOM Aug 5 2026; (5) China preliminary anti-dumping on Japanese chip chemical (DCS), MOFCOM Sep 8 2026; (6) US Commerce AD/CVD determination on Chinese L-lysine + spray-foam circumvention inquiry, Federal Register Jul 23-24 2026. items.fact: MOFCOM Nov-7-2025 suspension of Oct-9 rare-earth controls remains in force until Nov 10, 2026 (primary: whitehouse.gov fact-sheet Nov-5-2025; MOFCOM Announcements 70/72). Modern Diplomacy (Aug 21 2026) frames the truce as 'increasingly resembling a pause' with Beijing unlikely to extend, suggesting trajectory toward 2

items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: The regime is case-by-case per shipment for most exporters, general licences are whitelisted to named producers only (not broadly available), processing times routinely exceed 30 days (60–120 days observed), and new categories (samarium, gadolinium, lutetium compounds) were added to the control list within the trailing 3 months of the Jan 2026 catalogue update — all three rubric triggers for Score 1 (SLOWING) are met. Score 2 is not warranted because licences are still being issued across civilian/automotive end-users and no categorical denial or formal suspension of licensing has been announced.
items.fact: As of September 2026, China's April 2025 MOFCOM export licensing regime (Announcement No. 18) remains fully in force for seven medium/heavy rare earth elements and downstream magnets (NdFeB containing Dy/Tb, SmCo). Licensing is case-by-case per shipment; general licences exist but are available only to a small whitelist of named Chinese producers (e.g. JL MAG, Zhongke Sanhuan, Ningbo Yunsheng, issued Dec 2025) and are not broadly available. Processing times routinely run 60–120 days in practice, well above the 45-working-day statutory target. The January 2026 Export Licensing Catalogue added samarium, gadolinium, and lutetium compounds as new controlled categories. The October 2025 expansion (extraterritorial/0.1% rule) remains suspended until 10–27 November 2026 under MOFCOM Announcements No. 70/72 (2025). Sources: gettransport.com logistics guide (Jul 7 2026); rare-earth-mining.com buyer guide (Apr 16 2026); certivo.com (Mar 11 2026); techtimes.com (May 27 2026).

dissent.view: Rare Earth Exchanges (Apr 2026) cites licensing approval rates below 25% for European firms in some sectors, which some analysts read as approaching a functional freeze for those buyers — closer to Score 2 for defence/advanced-tech applicants.

items.label: Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

The only overseas <=3nm fabs (Arizona Phase 2, Kumamoto Phase 2) are in equipment-install or construction phase with volume production 1-2 years away.
items.fact: As of Q3 2026, TSMC's entire <=3nm capacity (~260,000+ wpm combined 2nm+3nm) is in Taiwan. One analyst projection estimates sub-2nm capacity will split '70% Taiwan and 30% US by 2030' — a forward projection, not a 2026 figure.

items.label: AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)
items.rationale: Queues are massive, lengthening, and causing multi-year project delays for power - squarely matching rubric band 1 (TIGHT). FERC's June 2026 emergency action confirms the severity, but the absence of any confirmed curtailment of data-center load or a declared grid emergency prevents escalation to band 2 (ACUTE).
items.fact: As of end-2025/early-2026, U.S. interconnection queues held ~1,312 GW of generation + ~749 GW of storage across ~8,200 active projects (LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition, emp.lbl.gov, data through end-2025); ERCOT alone received 198 GW of large-load applications in Q1 2026, with data centers comprising ~87% of ERCOT's 410 GW large-load queue; interconnection wait times in the busiest U.S. markets run 4-7 years. No confirmed forced curtailment of data-center load or declared grid emergency has been reported.

dissent.view: Some secondary sources cite 2,600 GW in total U.S. queues as of early 2026, likely combining generation, storage, and large-load requests across all queue types, versus LBNL's more conservative 1,312 GW generation + 749 GW storage figure based on ISO/RTO filings through end-2025.

items.label: Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: The rubric's Level 2 threshold requires 'a statewide moratorium enacted OR >10 jurisdictions with enacted pauses/cancellations.' New York's signed executive order alone clears the statewide bar; the 100+ local moratoria across 25 states independently clears the >10-jurisdiction bar. Both conditions are met simultaneously with confirmed physical permit blockages.

Additionally, Texas Governor Abbott ordered a statewide grid audit in August 2026 effectively pausing new projects (multistate.us, Aug 19, 2026). DLA Piper (July 1, 2026) counts 56 public actions across 25 states and 100+ local moratoria enacted nationwide.

dissent.view: Maine's legislature passed a moratorium in April 2026, which would have been the first statewide enactment, but Gov. Janet Mills vetoed it — so Maine does not count as enacted.

New York's Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560), passed by the legislature June 4, 2026, has not been signed into law by Hochul — the operative action is the July 14 executive order, not the statute.

items.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)

items.label: Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

No confirmed deliberate physical flow cut-off has been carried out, so level 2 is not warranted.
items.fact: India has held the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty 'in abeyance' since April 2025 and continues to do so as of September 2026. On 31 August 2026, the Permanent Court of Arbitration at The Hague ruled the treaty 'remains fully in force' and India has no right to suspend it; India rejected the award as 'null and void' and reaffirmed the abeyance. Pakistan has stopped receiving routine river-flow data and site inspections since 2023; the Permanent Indus Commission has not met since May 2022. Pakistan's defence minister warned in June 2026 that water is a national security issue but said current developments do not yet warrant military action. No confirmed deliberate physical flow cut-off has been carried out. (Sources: Al Jazeera 2026-09-01, CNBC 2026-09-01, Britannica updated 2026-09-12, Chatham House 2026-04-17)

dissent.view: GERD/Nile dispute also sits at level 1: diplomacy frozen, Egypt raising issue at UNSC, Ethiopia announcing three new Blue Nile dams in March 2026, but no kinetic action or confirmed flow cut-off (New Arab, JURIST April 2026)

items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: Lecornu II holds no working majority and has repeatedly relied on Socialist/conservative forbearance to survive no-confidence votes — textbook rubric 1 (FRAGILE). No confidence vote has been lost and no dissolution called, so rubric 2 (COLLAPSE) does not apply.
items.fact: The Second Lecornu government (incumbent, formed 10 Oct 2025) is a minority coalition governing without a working majority. It has survived multiple no-confidence votes — most recently on 2 Feb 2026, when two motions (far-left: 260 votes; far-right: 135 votes) fell well short of the 289 required, allowing the 2026 budget to pass. No dissolution or snap election has been called. Sources: Al Jazeera (2 Feb 2026 https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/2/france-adopts-2026-budget-after-two-no-confidence-votes-fail), Wikipedia Lecornu governments (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecornu_governments), Euronews (23 Jan 2026 https://www.euronews.com/2026/01/23/french-government-avoids-collapse-after-surviving-two-no-confidence-votes).

items.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
items.rationale: The trustees report materially worsened the OASI depletion date and the long-term funding gap, and reform legislation is actively debated in both chambers -- satisfying the rubric's DEBATE criterion (band 1). No automatic cut has been triggered (trust fund not yet depleted) and no legislation enacting cuts has been enacted, so band 2 is not met.
items.fact: The 2026 SSA Trustees Report (issued June 9, 2026) projects the OASI trust fund depleted in Q4 2032 -- one quarter earlier than the 2025 report -- with the 75-year actuarial deficit widening to 4.42% of taxable payroll (source: ssa.gov/oact/trsum/, June 2026). No benefit cut has been enacted; Congress is debating but has not passed the Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act of 2026 (H.R. 9187) or the PROMISE Act (S. 4979).

items.label: USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
items.rationale: The IMF COFER Q1 2026 release is the most recent official data point; 57.13% maps directly to the rubric requiring the latest USD share of allocated global FX reserves as a percent. The figure is confirmed by multiple IMF-sourced secondary outlets with no material deviation.
items.fact: IMF COFER Data Brief (published ~June 30, 2026): 'The share of US dollar holdings in foreign exchange reserves increased to 57.13 percent in 2026Q1, from 56.42 percent in 2025Q4.' Source: https://data.imf.org/en/news/imf%20data%20brief%20july%201

items.label: Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)
items.rationale: Multiple corroborating sources from mid-to-late 2026 converge on a 4x–5x ex-China premium for the canonical HREE benchmark (dysprosium oxide); 4.5 is the midpoint of that observed range and is supported by both Argus price data and Benchmark Minerals' 2025 baseline of 4.4x trending higher into 2026.
items.fact: Dysprosium oxide trades at $205–211/kg inside China vs $575–$1,100+/kg ex-China (floor-to-spot range), implying a 2.7x–5.2x multiple; Argus data cited by Reuters (June 2026) and REEx (Aug 6, 2026) characterise the dysprosium/terbium ex-China premium as '4x to 5x' domestic Chinese prices. Benchmark Minerals (March 24, 2026) reported 2025 dysprosium CIF North America at 4.4x EXW China. Sources: rareearthexchanges.com (Aug 6 2026), theoregongroup.com citing Argus/Reuters (June 10 2026), source.benchmarkminerals.com (March 24 2026).

items.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: Persistent PRC coast guard and naval patrols at record vessel counts plus a live-fire drill in July 2026 constitute assertive, large-scale pressure short of a kinetic clash or blockade, squarely matching rubric level 1 (ELEVATED). Aerial ADIZ incursions are trending down from 2024-2025 peaks, providing no market-disruption or blockade signal to support a level-2 read.
items.fact: ISW/AEI China & Taiwan Update (Sept 1, 2026): PLA carried out 125 aerial incursions into Taiwan's ADIZ in August 2026 — less than half the August 2024/2025 totals — while Taiwan's CGA recorded a record 244 PRC vessels in Taiwanese waters in July and 1,247 PRC vessels near Taiwan and its outlying islands since May 2026, with the PRC conducting persistent patrols east of Taiwan since May. The most recent named drill event was a two-day PLA live-fire exercise in the Taiwan Strait (Jul 24-25, 2026, per SCMP/MSA navigation warning). No kinetic clash or actual blockade has been reported.

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc.) appear on the MOFCOM export-control list by firm name, not as a sector class, mapping directly to rubric value 1. Benchmark Minerals explicitly characterises the measure as 'entity-specific rather than a blanket restriction on rare earth exports to the US', and market price signals were described as muted, consistent with a firm-specific rather than sector-wide action.
items.fact: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026, issued 22 June 2026, added 10 named US entities to China's export control list; the two US rare-earth producers explicitly named are MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc. The other eight entities are defense/drone/aerospace firms (Aveox, Red Cat Holdings, Teal Drones, IMSAR, Jaia Robotics, Ball Aerospace, Oshkosh Defense, L3Harris Maritime Services). The measure is firm-specific, not a categorical ban on the US rare-earth sector. Sources: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 as reported by GlobalSecurity.org (citing Global Times, 22 Jun 2026); Benchmark Minerals (25 Jun 2026); Bloomberg (22 Jun 2026); Al Jazeera (22 Jun 2026).

items.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: Index is rising and at a multi-year high, but the MoM gain (+1.9%) is below the 3% upper bound for Band 1; the 3-month rise (~May 130.7 to Aug 133.3, ~+2%) is far below the 10% SPIKING threshold. Rubric maps squarely to ELEVATED (1).
items.fact: FAO FFPI averaged 133.3 points in August 2026, up 1.9% MoM from revised July level of 130.8 and +2.5% YoY, reaching its highest level since late 2022. Source: FAO newsroom (fao.org), released 4 September 2026.

flags.name: Redemption gates widespread, but HY spreads benign
flags.message: Large-fund redemption gates are rated WIDESPREAD (2) but high-yield spreads are benign. Broad gating usually coincides with visible credit stress; confirm the gates are systemic, not a couple of isolated funds.

indicators.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

s1_basis_trade.label: Hidden leverage in US government bonds
s1_basis_trade.gist: Hedge funds borrow heavily to trade US government bonds; if that trade unwinds fast it can freeze the market everyone treats as safe.

s2_japan.label: Japan's rates and the global cash carry trade
s2_japan.gist: Cheap Japanese money has funded bets worldwide for years; as Japan's interest rates rise, pulling that money home can ripple through global markets.

s3_private_credit.label: Private lending you can't see into
s3_private_credit.gist: A fast-growing pile of loans sits outside the banks with little public disclosure, so stress there is hard to spot until it is already large.

s4_dev_debt.label: Debt stress in developing countries
s4_dev_debt.gist: Many poorer nations owe more than they can comfortably repay; a wave of defaults can spread and pull in their lenders.

s5_china_deflation.label: China's prices spilling into the world
s5_china_deflation.gist: Big swings in China's factory prices - falling or rising - get exported to everyone else as cheaper goods or higher input costs.

s6_rare_earths.label: Rare-earth minerals used as a weapon
s6_rare_earths.gist: China controls most of the world's rare-earth processing and is now restricting it, squeezing US defense and high-tech manufacturing.

s7_stablecoins.label: Crypto dollars and US government debt
s7_stablecoins.gist: Stablecoins must hold US Treasuries as backing, so their rapid growth - or a sudden wobble - now feeds straight back into the government-debt market.

s8_ai_capex.label: The AI spending boom
s8_ai_capex.gist: Enormous borrowing to build AI data centers is racing ahead of the revenue meant to justify it, concentrating the risk in a few giant companies.

s9_cre.label: Commercial real estate and small banks
s9_cre.gist: Half-empty offices and loans coming due strain the regional banks that hold them - a slow-burning credit risk.

s10_france.label: France and eurozone stability
s10_france.gist: A politically gridlocked, heavily indebted France is the soft spot that could reopen broader euro-area stress.

s11_consumer_debt.label: Household debt strain
s11_consumer_debt.gist: Rising late payments on car loans and buy-now-pay-later show households stretching - an early warning on consumer health.

s12_gold_dedollar.label: Gold and moving away from the dollar
s12_gold_dedollar.gist: Central banks stockpiling gold and building non-dollar payment systems slowly chip away at the dollar's dominance.

s13_insurance.label: Insurers pulling back
s13_insurance.gist: As disaster losses climb, insurers raise prices or quit whole regions, leaving homes and assets exposed.

s14_pensions.label: Pensions and an aging population
s14_pensions.gist: Aging populations and underfunded pensions strain public budgets; leveraged pension funds can also break in a sudden rate shock, as the UK saw in 2022.

s15_ai_power.label: AI's strain on the power grid
s15_ai_power.gist: AI data centers need more electricity than the grid can quickly supply, triggering curtailments, building moratoria, and multi-year connection queues.

s16_copper.label: Copper for electrification
s16_copper.gist: Electrifying everything needs far more copper than mines can deliver, and major mine outages are tightening supply further.

s17_water.label: Water as a hidden constraint
s17_water.gist: Droughts and shrinking reservoirs threaten chip factories, farms, and power generation - an underpriced input with no substitute.

s18_food_fertilizer.label: Food and fertilizer supply
s18_food_fertilizer.gist: Export curbs and shipping disruptions to fertilizer raise the risk of higher food prices down the line.

s19_lithography.label: The chipmaking chokepoint
s19_lithography.gist: The most advanced chips depend on one Dutch tool-maker and Taiwan's factories; any disruption there hits the entire tech economy.

s20_sea_lanes.label: Shipping lanes and undersea cables
s20_sea_lanes.gist: Key straits like Hormuz and the undersea cables carrying the internet are vulnerable chokepoints for global trade and data.

s21_clearinghouses.label: The financial system's plumbing
s21_clearinghouses.gist: Clearinghouses sit at the center of every market; if one seized up under stress, it would jam trading everywhere at once.

playbook.disclaimer: Educational cause-and-effect only - how stress like this has historically moved through the system. Nothing here is investment advice or a prediction.

s1_basis_trade.mechanism: A rates shock forces highly leveraged government-bond arbitrage positions to unwind at once: margin calls trigger forced Treasury selling, liquidity in the world's benchmark market evaporates, and everything priced off it reprices.
benefits: cash and short-term bills through the panic
long-term government bonds AFTER central-bank intervention
s1_basis_trade.watch: The funding-spread and bond-volatility rows above; the historical pivot was the central bank announcing a backstop facility.
s1_basis_trade.trap: In past episodes the 'safe' asset itself fell first - forced sellers sell what they can - so the flight-to-safety instinct lost money until the intervention.

s2_japan.mechanism: Surging Japanese yields pull decades of cheap yen funding home: the yen spikes on repatriation, and leveraged positions worldwide that were financed in yen get liquidated together - hitting high-momentum equities and emerging markets hardest.
benefits: Japanese banks and insurers as rates normalize
s2_japan.watch: The 30-year JGB row above (live official feed) and the yen; past unwinds announced themselves through the currency.
s2_japan.trap: Historical carry unwinds were violent but brief - the 2024 episode round-tripped within days; the durable shift was in Japanese financials, not the panic.

s3_private_credit.mechanism: One honest markdown forces everyone's marks: investor withdrawals hit gates, gated funds fire-sell into an illiquid market, and lending to mid-sized companies contracts just as they need to refinance.
bleeds: private-credit vehicles trading below stated asset value
benefits: holders of dry powder buying discounted credit afterwards
public high-quality credit as the flight destination
s3_private_credit.watch: The default-rate and redemption-gate rows above; public high-yield spreads are the honest proxy for hidden marks.
s3_private_credit.trap: Opacity means the repricing arrives as a sudden gap, not a trend - by the time it is public, the move has largely happened.

s4_dev_debt.mechanism: A cluster of sovereign defaults - not one - overwhelms the restructuring machinery: redemptions from emerging-market debt funds force indiscriminate selling of strong and weak credits alike, and stress spreads through common creditors.
benefits: and historically the buyers of defaulted debt after restructuring - among the best-documented recoveries in fixed income
s4_dev_debt.watch: The new-IMF-programs row above and the dollar's strength, which is usually the upstream cause.
s4_dev_debt.trap: Index diversification means one or two defaults barely register; the systemic wave this story warns of is exactly what official bailouts exist to prevent.

s5_china_deflation.mechanism: Deepening factory-gate deflation is exported as cheaper goods, compressing margins for competing producers everywhere - unless Beijing's stimulus response whipsaws the pressure into a sudden commodity and China-equity rebound.
benefits: long-term bonds in the deflation leg
Chinese equities and industrial metals in the stimulus leg
s5_china_deflation.watch: The producer-price row above and any stimulus announcement - the two legs point opposite directions.
s5_china_deflation.trap: Policy whipsaw: historically every stimulus rumor violently reversed the deflation trade within days.

s6_rare_earths.mechanism: Export restrictions tighten into denial: magnet and heavy-rare-earth supply to defense, vehicle, and robotics manufacturers halts, panic stockpiling begins, and processing capacity outside China re-rates from commodity business to strategic asset.
bleeds: vehicle and defense production schedules in the short run
s6_rare_earths.watch: The license-flow, blacklist, and ex-China premium rows above - the premium is the market's own severity gauge.
s6_rare_earths.trap: Historically these moves reversed as fast as they started on any truce headline, and diversified funds in the space often hold the Chinese producers too.

s7_stablecoins.mechanism: A run on a major stablecoin forces its reserves - tens of billions in short-term government debt - to liquidate within days, briefly dislocating the bill market while the crypto ecosystem's dollar rails seize and leveraged positions cascade.
benefits: historically the surviving issuer gained lasting market share after each depeg scare
s7_stablecoins.watch: The live peg-deviation and supply rows above (updated daily from the aggregator) - past runs announced themselves in the peg first.
s7_stablecoins.trap: Crypto markets have a long history of face-ripping rebounds inside downtrends; past episodes punished conviction in both directions.

s8_ai_capex.mechanism: The debt-financed buildout meets a revenue shortfall: one credit event at a leveraged data-center operator reprices all AI-adjacent borrowing, capital-spending guidance gets cut, chip orders fall, and power-demand forecasts deflate - the whole complex moves together because it was funded together.
bleeds: power producers priced on AI demand
benefits: and - the dot-com lesson - the post-bust survivors compounded for a decade
s8_ai_capex.watch: The capex-gap, revenue-gap, and refinancing rows above; credit stress historically led equity repricing.
s8_ai_capex.trap: Bubbles run longer than solvency: betting against this one early has been the era's classic ruin trade, which is why timing signals matter more than valuation.

s9_cre.mechanism: Office refinancing failures cluster into bank failures: deposit flight spreads to lookalike regional lenders, credit to small business contracts, and commercial-property marks finally reflect reality.
benefits: the largest banks via deposit inflows
and historically the whole sector rebounded within days of a backstop
s9_cre.watch: The bank-failure and office-delinquency rows above and the official problem-bank list.
s9_cre.trap: The 2023 backstop bottomed the sector in 48 hours - the policy response, not the failure, was the historical turning point.

s10_france.mechanism: Fiscal paralysis pushes French borrowing costs through crisis thresholds: banks holding the government's own bonds absorb the losses, the sovereign-bank doom loop reawakens, and stress spreads across euro-area borrowing costs.
bleeds: other high-debt euro members through contagion
benefits: and non-euro safe havens in every euro crisis
s10_france.watch: The OAT-Bund spread row above (live feed) - it is the market's single-number verdict on this story.
s10_france.trap: The central bank: euro-breakup positioning has been ruined repeatedly by ECB backstops built precisely for this scenario.

s11_consumer_debt.mechanism: Subprime stress spreads upward: rising late payments become charge-offs, lenders tighten, discretionary spending cracks, and the weakness travels from consumer lenders to retailers to the broad economy.
benefits: trade-down retailers in every past consumer squeeze
s11_consumer_debt.watch: The subprime-delinquency and BNPL rows above; the staples-versus-discretionary ratio is the market's own recession gauge.
s11_consumer_debt.trap: Lenders provision ahead of losses - their shares historically bottomed while delinquencies were still rising.

s12_gold_dedollar.mechanism: A reserve-weaponization event accelerates the slow shift: central banks swap dollar assets for gold at a faster pace, marginal foreign demand for government debt weakens, and the metal gains a structural, price-insensitive buyer.
bleeds: long-term government bonds via lost foreign demand
benefits: gold above all - the current central-bank buying era is the live example - plus non-dollar safe havens
s12_gold_dedollar.watch: The reserve-share row above (quarterly official data) and central-bank purchase reports.
s12_gold_dedollar.trap: This is measured in decades, not events - and gold miners have historically lagged the metal itself across full cycles.

s13_insurance.mechanism: A mega-catastrophe season collides with insurers already exiting exposed regions: property becomes uninsurable, collateral values fall, and the stress transmits to mortgages, regional lenders, and state backstops.
bleeds: property values and lenders in exposed regions
benefits: historically reinsurers AFTER the event as pricing hardened
and catastrophe-linked debt yields for risk-bearers
s13_insurance.watch: The insurer-exit and catastrophe-loss rows above plus the season's forecasts.
s13_insurance.trap: Positioning before the event absorbs the loss; the well-documented historical pattern favored the post-event hard market.

s14_pensions.mechanism: A rate spike forces leveraged pension strategies into collateral calls: they dump whatever is liquid, the selling pushes yields higher still, and the spiral continues until a central bank steps in - the UK lived this in 2022.
bleeds: long-term government bonds during the spiral itself
retirees' security in the slow version
benefits: whoever provided liquidity at the intervention - the 2022 central-bank entry marked the exact bottom - and retirement insurers structurally as rates rose
s14_pensions.watch: The funded-ratio row above (live monthly feed) and long-bond volatility.
s14_pensions.trap: Identical to the basis trade: buying the falling 'safe' asset before the intervention caught knives for days.

s15_ai_power.mechanism: Data-center demand outruns the grid so badly that curtailments, connection queues, and building moratoria stall the buildout - rising household bills turn it political, and the constraint moves from engineering to consent.
bleeds: utilities caught between regulators and demand
benefits: and nuclear/gas capacity - though see the trap
s15_ai_power.watch: The interconnection-wait and moratoria rows above and capacity-auction prices.
s15_ai_power.trap: The famous version of this trade assumes the buildout CONTINUES; this story's actual blow-up - moratoria stopping it - points the opposite way for the same names.

s16_copper.mechanism: A structural deficit meets a supply shock - a major mine closure removes years of planned supply - and the metal prices high enough to ration demand, raising costs for every grid, vehicle, and data-center project simultaneously.
benefits: producing miners with volume to sell
s16_copper.watch: The mine-disruption and deficit rows above and exchange inventory levels.
s16_copper.trap: The political risk that causes the shocks sits inside the producers themselves - the closed mine may be the one you were counting on.

s17_water.mechanism: Severe drought hits a chip hub, a farm belt, and cooling-dependent power at once: an unpriced input becomes a binding constraint, cutting industrial output regionally and feeding into food prices.
benefits: historically crop prices in drought years
s17_water.watch: The reservoir and drought rows above (live official feed for the largest US reservoir).
s17_water.trap: There is no pure play - broad 'water' funds are mostly global industrials, while the shock is local; the honest effects are second-order.

s18_food_fertilizer.mechanism: Fertilizer export restrictions cut application in poorer countries, next season's yields fall, grain prices spike, and food inflation becomes social and fiscal stress in import-dependent nations - looping back into the developing-world debt story.
benefits: fertilizer producers in every past squeeze
s18_food_fertilizer.watch: The FAO food-price row above (live feed) and the export-curb indicator.
s18_food_fertilizer.trap: Fertilizer stress historically reversed violently when curbs lifted, taking back most of the move.

s19_lithography.mechanism: Conflict or blockade around Taiwan stops the fabs that make nearly all leading-edge chips: every electronics supply chain seizes within a quarter, and the shock is large enough that markets themselves may not function normally.
bleeds: and anything with a chip in it
s19_lithography.watch: The tension and export-control rows above; false-alarm cycles have historically outnumbered real escalations many times over.
s19_lithography.trap: In the true scenario, settlement and market access are themselves at risk - analysis that assumes functioning markets may not apply.

s20_sea_lanes.mechanism: A chokepoint closes - this board just watched Hormuz do it - and shipping rates, war-risk insurance, and energy prices spike together while longer reroutes quietly shrink effective global capacity; cable cuts do the same for data.
s20_sea_lanes.watch: The live strait-transit feed and cable-incident rows above.
s20_sea_lanes.trap: This board's own history shows it: reopening headlines crushed the shipping move within days - persistence of the disruption was everything.

s21_clearinghouses.mechanism: A major member defaults into a volatile market and the clearinghouse's loss waterfall activates: surviving members face assessments and de-risk simultaneously, margin requirements spiral procyclically, and the plumbing everyone assumed away becomes the crisis itself.
benefits: almost nothing leveraged - which is the honest answer; cash
and physical assets have no counterparty
s21_clearinghouses.watch: The clearing-mandate rollout row above and any clearinghouse margin announcements.
s21_clearinghouses.trap: The deepest on the board: in a true clearing failure, a winning derivative position may itself not pay out.

context.intro: The famous dials, for contrast. These are the most-watched macro gauges in the world - shown here so you can compare them with this tracker's structural lens. They are not part of the score. When they disagree with the gauge above, that divergence is the story: markets price these continuously, while the risks this tracker follows are the kind markets historically ignored until they ruptured.

items.label: VIX
items.note: Expected US stock-market volatility - the most-watched fear gauge. Calm markets usually sit below ~20.

items.label: 10y-2y curve
items.note: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield. A negative (inverted) reading has historically preceded US recessions - with long and variable lags.

items.label: High-yield spread
items.note: The extra yield markets demand to lend to risky companies - the market's own price of credit stress. Calm is roughly below ~4.

items.label: Chicago Fed NFCI
items.note: The Chicago Fed's broad financial-conditions index across money, debt, and equity markets. Negative = looser (calmer) than average.

items.label: Unemployment
items.note: The US unemployment rate - the classic real-economy dial, updated monthly.
